claims.claim: The organization has promised ApplicationSet teardown twice and incompatibly: the roadmap states that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, while the PRD introduces a `deletionOrder` field on `ApplicationSetStrategy` whose `Reverse` value deletes children in reverse `rollingSync` step order and waits for each to be fully deleted. Both cannot hold; the incident review explicitly leaves this disagreement unowned ('needs an owner. not deciding here'), so no one currently owns retiring the roadmap's out-of-scope statement.

Impersonation's enablement granularity is committed two ways. RFC-001 states as a goal that the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level and that once set it applies to all Argo CD Applications, and its examples enable it by patching `application.sync.impersonation.enabled` in `argocd-cm`. The platform sync call recorded the opposite as a firm decision: rollout goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide, with no project flipped until the diff story is fixed. A per-project gate cannot be built on a system-level-only switch; the RFC's goal or the rollout decision has to give.

The PRD's risk assessment is falsified by field evidence on the very mechanism it ships. The PRD records 'No immediate Risks to consider' and describes `Reverse` as waiting for one application to be fully deleted before moving to the next. T-28511 reports that exact wait never completing when a child is stuck in `Progressing`, with the controller restarting the wave from the top and the Application flipping between Deleting and Syncing indefinitely. The blocking-wait semantics the PRD treats as risk-free are the mechanism of the reported loop.

The PRD commits to two incompatible handling rules for an unsupported `deletionOrder` value. Its Implementation Details require a check correlating the deletion strategy to the ApplicationSet strategy that errors out when the order cannot be honored; its Non-Goals commit to a UI that accepts the `custom` value in the field and silently ignores it. The roadmap closes the escape route: first-class ApplicationSet UI/CLI/API support is stated as not including management of child deletion order, so no interface surface owns raising that error.

A roadmap request depends on the capability the roadmap declared out of scope. T-24578 asks for Source Hydrator support on ApplicationSets with the stated motivation of controlling destroy ordering of Applications across multiple ApplicationSets, whose current absence forces an app-of-apps-per-cluster workaround to regain sync waves. The roadmap states ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented, so the ticket's motivating outcome is unreachable through the ApplicationSet path it proposes, and the app-of-apps indirection it wants to remove is the only sanctioned teardown mechanism.

T-24578 asks for exactly the combination the incident review banned. The review's interim call is that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, because each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. T-24578 proposes hydrating ApplicationSet-generated Applications into a Git repo that an app-of-apps then syncs, which puts hydrator pushes and progressive-sync waves in the same loop by design rather than by accident, making the restriction a scope constraint on the feature, not just on the pilot.

Ordered deletion is being staffed by moving people off its own recovery path. The platform sync call deprioritizes the hydrator History & Rollback work to next quarter and moves the dev pair onto the progressive sync deletion loop. T-27327 is the ticket that would give hydrator-backed applications a rollback that renders directly to the sync branch. Shipping `deletionOrder: Reverse`, which deletes sequentially and can stall partway as T-28511 shows, therefore lands with no automated way to restore the manifests for the children already deleted.

RFC-001's central promise — that the control plane's standing credential is used purely for control plane operations while sync runs as the destination service account, achieving least privilege — does not hold on the diff path. T-28695 reports that Server-Side Diff ignores the AppProject's `destinationServiceAccounts` and runs as the cluster Secret credential, and because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, computing a diff requires real `patch` authority on every resource kind in the Application. The privilege the RFC removed from sync reappears, unbounded, on the credential the RFC claimed to narrow.

T-26271 and the platform sync call describe the same defect from opposite ends and neither says so. The reporter observes CI `argocd app diff` failures in the projects where the sync impersonation flag was recently enabled and cannot reconcile the narrow identity with a broad cluster Secret credential; the call root-caused it as diff running as the destination service account, which lacks `patch` on cluster-scoped resources. The root cause was never written onto the ticket, so the reporter is still chasing the cluster Secret and the false-positive diff it produces stays a live risk of unintended modification on sync.

The stable-promotion gate for Progressive Sync has no data to decide on. T-28927 defines the remaining scope for promoting Progressive Sync from beta to Stable under a definition requiring the feature be tested and validated across use cases, while T-27846 records that getting a wide-eye view of progressive sync is still difficult and that metrics answering how long a step took, what a sync is waiting on, and how many refreshes an ApplicationSet caused are an open proposal. Maturity is being judged without the instrumentation that would show it.

The only completion signal available for the PRD's deletion ordering is one that is already known to lie. The PRD's `Reverse` order depends on `rollingSync` step progression to sequence work, and T-27949 shows `status.applicationStatus` reporting a rollout complete and `Healthy` while child Applications are `OutOfSync` and no sync operation was created, because a `Waiting` status is promoted back to `Healthy` off the pre-update child state. A deletion wave that stalls will report the same way, so 'it worked' cannot be established from ApplicationSet status.

The PRD's validation rule has no meaning under the parallel-step model being proposed. The PRD requires that `Reverse` be selectable only when `rollingSync` lists an order of deployment, and derives deletion order by inverting that step list. T-28755 proposes `parallel` step groups (or `parallelGroups`) precisely so that logically independent clusters are not sequential barriers, which leaves the step list without a total order to reverse. Either `Reverse` must reject parallel groups or its inversion semantics are undefined for them.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode is stated as the integration point on which an automated environment promotion system can be built, and building such a system on it is Goal 2 — while implementing promotion is a declared Non-Goal, leaving the mover external. T-26443 reports that in push-to-stage mode auto-sync deploys whatever the stage branch last held before the external promoter moves fresh manifests, and the platform sync call records that the organization's own stage-branch promoter is still an unowned shell script. The mode's safety rests entirely on a component the RFC excluded from scope and no one owns.

T-27327 proposes that rollback write directly to the sync branch, bypassing the staging branch, in both hydrator modes, on the argument that single-application rollbacks do not fit promotion flows. RFC-002 defines push-to-stage as the mode in which manifests go to a different branch and an external system moves them to the deployment branch, and makes building a promotion system on that mode an explicit goal. A sanctioned write path that bypasses the stage branch breaks the invariant that every change to the deployment branch passes through promotion.

The pilot in T-27949 violates RFC-002's stated opinions on the same repository where it runs the hydrator. RFC-002 lists config tool parameter overrides in the Application `spec.source` fields as nondeterministic external configuration that hydration reproducibility locks out, and requires every deployed change to have a corresponding dry commit. T-27949's ApplicationSet drives child Applications through generated `spec.source.helm.parameters` that change with no change in `targetRevision`, on a repo where the hydrator is being piloted, so the change that moves desired state originates outside the dry branch.
